strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem for GUI agents: domain-specific workflow and grounding bias in real software. The proposed framing into planning-level and grounding-level bias is clear and useful.

GUIDE is a practical training-free systems contribution, even though no contribution type is explicitly declared. I would assess it as Applied/Systems rather than a purely algorithmic paper; under that lens, the plug-and-play integration with single-model and multi-agent GUI agents is a meaningful contribution.

The method is well motivated: subtitle-driven retrieval, inverse-dynamics-style frame-pair annotation, UI element parsing, and natural-language planning/grounding injection form a coherent pipeline for converting tutorial videos into task-specific knowledge.

Experiments on OSWorld are reasonably broad, covering 361 tasks and three agent settings. The reported gains are consistent: +7.48 for Seed-1.8, +5.83 for Qwen3-VL-8B, and +4.47 for AgentS3, suggesting the approach is not tied to one executor.

The ablations support the main design choices: planning knowledge accounts for most gains, grounding adds complementary value in UI-heavy domains, and annotation model quality matters but even weaker annotators improve over no annotation.

The paper includes useful diagnostics beyond headline scores, including retrieval coverage, human evaluation of GUI-video classification and topic extraction, cost analysis, and concrete failure cases where retrieved videos mislead the agent.
weaknesses: The empirical comparison to prior work is not fully convincing. Watch&Learn is only compared via an aggregate number on a different agent/baseline, and other relevant retrieval/tutorial systems are not evaluated under the same OSWorld protocol. This makes it hard to isolate GUIDE's advantage over simpler video/text RAG baselines.

Reproducibility is a major concern. The system relies on live YouTube search, dynamic video availability, subtitles, yt-dlp behavior, proprietary OpenAI models, GPT-5.1/GPT-5.2-style components, Seed-1.8 APIs, and model-specific prompting. Without released cached retrieval results, videos, prompts, annotations, and execution logs, reproducing the exact benchmark may be difficult.

The evaluation does not sufficiently control for retrieval confounds. Missing baselines include title-only retrieval, subtitle retrieval without inverse-dynamics annotation, web-text tutorial RAG, random/topical video references, and using only raw subtitles as context. These controls are needed to prove that the proposed three-stage Video-RAG and annotation pipeline, rather than generic task-conditioned external knowledge, drive the gains.

The final relevance matching stage and procedural consistency are weakly validated. Human studies evaluate GUI classification and topic extraction, but not whether selected videos actually match the target task workflow. The paper's own failure cases show that semantically adjacent but procedurally wrong videos can derail execution.

Some reported gains are modest or mixed at the domain level. Grounding often adds less than 1 point overall and can reduce performance in several domains, including the Multi category for Seed-1.8 and AgentS3. The paper would benefit from statistical confidence intervals or repeated trials, since GUI-agent evaluation can be noisy.

The ablations are limited: grounding-element count and annotator studies are conducted on a selected 50-task subset with complete annotations, which may overestimate the benefit relative to the full benchmark. There is also some inconsistency around the default grounding element count, with main experiments mentioning k=7 while some ablations and AgentS3 settings use k=5.

The approach may exploit public benchmark/task knowledge indirectly via task-conditioned web retrieval. This is not necessarily invalid for a retrieval-augmented agent, but the paper should discuss benchmark contamination and whether YouTube tutorials or web content cover OSWorld tasks unusually well.

The method has practical and ethical/legal dependencies that are under-discussed: using YouTube tutorials at inference time raises questions about content licensing, availability, privacy, API costs/latency, and robustness to adversarial or low-quality instructional videos.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem for GUI agents: domain-specific workflow and grounding failures when operating real software. The distinction between planning-level and grounding-level domain bias is clear and useful.

The proposed system is ambitious and reasonably well motivated: test-time retrieval of public tutorial videos, subtitle-based filtering, automated keyframe/UI-element annotation, and prompt-based injection into different GUI-agent architectures form a coherent applied/systems contribution.

The evaluation is broader than many GUI-agent papers, covering OSWorld with 361 tasks and three agent configurations. The reported absolute gains of roughly 4.5-7.5 points are potentially meaningful if reproducible.

The paper includes useful ablations on planning vs. grounding, grounding element count, and annotation model choice, and it provides qualitative success and failure cases rather than presenting the method as uniformly reliable.
The appendices discuss retrieval coverage, annotation cost, and a human evaluation of some pipeline components, which helps expose practical tradeoffs.
weaknesses: The scientific case is weakened by inadequate controls for the central claim. The method combines many factors: YouTube retrieval, subtitles, VLM inverse-dynamics annotation, OmniParser UI graphs, prompt engineering, and stronger proprietary models. There is no convincing comparison to simpler baselines such as title-only YouTube retrieval, subtitle-only text RAG, directly feeding retrieved subtitles/plans, using raw video frames without the elaborate annotation pipeline, or retrieving web tutorials rather than videos.

Reproducibility is a major concern. The system depends on live YouTube search results, changing subtitles/videos, yt-dlp availability, multiple proprietary models, and stochastic settings with temperature 1.0. The paper does not provide enough information to recreate the exact retrieved videos, annotations, or execution conditions, so the headline OSWorld results may be difficult to verify.

The use of stronger proprietary models as annotators and planners complicates attribution. The gains for smaller agents may partly reflect distillation of task knowledge from GPT-5.1/GPT-4.1 through prompts rather than the proposed video-RAG mechanism itself. The paper does not isolate how much benefit comes from the models' own prior GUI knowledge versus retrieved video evidence.

The benchmark protocol risks contamination or task-specific leakage. OSWorld tasks are public and the system searches the open web at test time for tutorial videos that may closely match benchmark tasks. This may be acceptable for an applied retrieval system, but the paper should explicitly analyze whether retrieved content contains near-solutions to benchmark tasks and compare against non-video web search or text retrieval under the same conditions.

The reported gains are modest and uneven. Several domains regress or barely improve, especially for AgentS3 where Multi drops from 40.32 to 37.10, OS drops from 70.83 to 70.83/no gain, and some domains degrade substantially. No statistical significance, confidence intervals, repeated runs, or per-task analysis are provided, despite high variance in GUI-agent execution.

The ablation evidence is limited. Key ablations are on a 50-task subset selected for complete grounding annotations, which may bias results toward cases where the method works. The default grounding element count is also somewhat confusing: the main setup says k=7, while ablations peak at k=5 and AgentS3 uses k=5.

The retrieval quality evaluation does not fully support the method's claims. The human studies evaluate GUI classification and topic extraction, but not the most important stage: whether the final retrieved videos are procedurally appropriate for the target task. The failure cases show exactly this gap, with retrieved videos producing wrong workflows or irrelevant grounding.

The method is technically more of a prompt-and-pipeline integration than a clearly novel algorithm. The inverse-dynamics formulation is largely a VLM prompting procedure over frame pairs and UI detections; the equation adds little technical substance, and the novelty over Watch&Learn, video-guided agents, and retrieval-augmented GUI agents is incremental unless stronger controlled experiments establish the unique value of each component.

Claims such as 'resolves domain bias' and 'architecture-agnostic' are overstated. The method sometimes misleads agents, depends heavily on retrieval quality, and is demonstrated on a small set of architectures with custom prompt integrations. The evidence supports 'can improve some GUI agents under some conditions,' not a general resolution of domain bias.

Practical costs and latency are under-characterized. The paper reports API annotation costs but omits or downplays costs from running GUI agents, video downloading/transcription, OmniParser, repeated failed retrievals, wall-clock delay, and operational fragility. This matters because the method is positioned as real-time test-time adaptation.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem for GUI agents: domain-specific workflow and grounding gaps that persist even in strong general VLM agents. The planning/grounding framing is clear and useful.

Although no contribution type is declared, I view the paper primarily as an Applied/Systems contribution rather than a pure Algorithms/General paper. Under that lens, the value is in the end-to-end retrieval, annotation, and plug-and-play integration pipeline, and the evidence is reasonably strong.

GUIDE is technically well motivated: subtitle-driven video retrieval, inverse-dynamics-style frame-pair annotation, UI-element parsing, and natural-language knowledge injection fit together coherently and address plausible failure modes of GUI agents.

The empirical results are encouraging. On OSWorld, GUIDE improves Seed-1.8 by 7.48 points, Qwen3-VL-8B by 5.83 points, and AgentS3 by 4.47 points without fine-tuning, suggesting the method is not tied to a single agent architecture.

The paper includes useful ablations and diagnostics: planning-only vs planning+grounding, grounding element count, annotation model choice, per-domain breakdowns, retrieval coverage, human evaluation of GUI classification/topic extraction, meaningful-frame filtering, cost analysis, and concrete failure cases.

The failure analysis is unusually candid and helpful, showing cases where retrieved videos mislead the agent through procedural mismatch or irrelevant UI grounding. This increases confidence that the authors understand the system’s limitations.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is a significant concern. The pipeline depends on live YouTube retrieval, proprietary and/or future model APIs such as GPT-5.1/GPT-5.2 and Seed-1.8, and changing web content. Without a frozen retrieval corpus, prompts, retrieved video IDs, and generated annotations, exact reproduction will be difficult.

The comparison to prior video-based methods is not fully controlled. Watch&Learn is only compared at a high level and apparently with a different agent/backbone, so the claim of outperforming it by a large margin is suggestive but not decisive.

Several important retrieval ablations are missing or underdeveloped: title-only retrieval vs subtitle-driven retrieval, no dual-anchor topic repetition, different K values, and robustness to irrelevant-but-plausible tutorials. Since retrieval quality is the main failure mode, these controls would strengthen the causal case.

Grounding provides only modest gains in the full benchmark and sometimes hurts particular domains/configurations, especially multi-domain tasks and AgentS3’s cross-application category. The paper acknowledges noise but could better quantify when grounding should be suppressed.

Some ablations use a 50-task subset selected for complete grounding annotations, which may overstate gains relative to the full OSWorld distribution. Statistical uncertainty or repeated runs are not reported, despite possible variance in GUI-agent execution and model sampling.

The method introduces nontrivial latency, cost, and external-dependency overhead at inference time. The cost analysis is useful, but the practical deployment story remains dependent on network availability, API access, video licensing/platform stability, and software-version match between tutorials and target environments.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely problem: GUI agents often fail not because of generic visual-language incapability, but because they lack application-specific procedural and grounding knowledge. The framing into planning-level and grounding-level domain bias is clear and useful.

Although no contribution type is declared, the work is best assessed as an Applied/Systems contribution rather than a purely algorithmic one. Under that lens, the proposed system is compelling: real-time web video retrieval, subtitle-based filtering, VLM pairwise annotation, and plug-and-play prompt injection form a coherent end-to-end framework.

The experimental evidence is fairly broad. GUIDE improves three agent settings on OSWorld by +4.47 to +7.48 percentage points, transfers to WindowsAgentArena with larger reported gains, and includes channel ablations, retrieval controls, raw-trajectory controls, K sensitivity, and annotation-pipeline ablations.

The paper does a good job attributing where the gains come from. The results suggest planning knowledge is the dominant contributor, grounding is complementary, and raw in-context trajectories are less useful than structured planning/grounding decomposition.

The failure analysis is unusually concrete and helpful. The authors show cases where retrieval mismatch or non-screencast videos mislead the agent, which clarifies both the promise and fragility of the approach.
weaknesses: The system depends heavily on proprietary and very strong models for retrieval, annotation, decomposition, and sometimes execution. This makes it difficult to separate the contribution of GUIDE from the capabilities of GPT-5.1/GPT-5.2-style annotators and weakens reproducibility for the broader community.

The live YouTube retrieval setting is powerful but unstable. Results may vary over time with search rankings, video availability, subtitles, ASR quality, and benchmark-task leakage through public web tutorials. The paper would be stronger with a frozen retrieval corpus or a fully specified artifact for exact reproduction.

Comparisons to the closest systems are incomplete. The paper includes a Watch-and-Learn-style raw trajectory control, but does not directly compare against other GUI RAG/tutorial systems such as RAG-GUI, KG-RAG, OS-Symphony, or manually curated video-injection methods under matched compute and model budgets.

Full-benchmark results appear to be single runs despite stochastic agents and temperature=1.0. Some subset ablations use repeated seeds, but the main claims would be more convincing with confidence intervals or repeated OSWorld/WAA runs.

The method introduces nontrivial inference-time cost and latency, including video search, download, ASR/keyframe extraction, OmniParser, and many VLM calls. The cost analysis is useful, but the paper does not fully evaluate wall-clock feasibility in realistic interactive deployments where users expect fast responses.

Some reported tables and claims need cleanup. For example, Table 4's delta row appears inconsistent for the subtitle-only condition, and several per-domain results are non-monotonic or degraded despite improved overall averages. These issues do not invalidate the main trend, but they reduce confidence in the presentation.

The approach can actively harm agents when retrieval is semantically close but procedurally wrong, as shown in the failure cases. The current safeguards rely mostly on prompting the agent to treat knowledge as reference material, which is not a robust mechanism for detecting mismatched workflows.

strengths: The paper tackles a timely and important problem for GUI agents: adapting general VLM-based agents to application-specific workflows and UI layouts without fine-tuning. The decomposition into retrieval, video annotation, and planning/grounding injection is sensible and directly motivated by observed GUI-agent failure modes.

The experimental scope is broader than many GUI-agent papers: results are reported on the full OSWorld subset of 361 tasks, three agent configurations, and an additional WindowsAgentArena transfer setting. The reported absolute gains of +4.47 to +7.48 pp on OSWorld and larger gains on WAA suggest the approach can be useful in practice.

The paper includes several relevant controls: planning-only vs planning+grounding, grounding-only, a Watch&Learn-style raw-trajectory in-context baseline using the same retrieved videos, transcript-only and no-OmniParser ablations, retrieval matching controls, and human audits of retrieval/filtering stages. These make the empirical case more credible than a simple end-to-end comparison.

The discussion of failure cases is concrete and helpful. The examples show that procedurally mismatched videos and non-screencast/irrelevant UI grounding can actively harm the agent, which is an important limitation for deployment.
The method is largely training-free and modular. Expressing video-derived knowledge in natural language makes the approach relatively easy to integrate into different GUI-agent architectures.
weaknesses: The core technical novelty is limited. GUIDE is mostly an orchestration of existing components: YouTube search, subtitle-based LLM filtering, Whisper, MOG2 keyframe extraction, OmniParser, VLM pairwise prompting, and prompt injection. The paper frames this as a new autonomous learning paradigm, but the algorithmic contribution beyond pipeline design and prompt engineering is modest.

Reproducibility is a serious concern. The strongest annotation and agent components rely on proprietary or difficult-to-reproduce models such as GPT-5.1/GPT-5.2 and Seed-1.8, real-time YouTube retrieval, changing subtitles, API behavior, and network-dependent GUI tasks. Even with code release, exact replication may be fragile.

The main comparisons are incomplete. The paper does not directly compare against strong tutorial/RAG GUI-agent baselines such as RAG-GUI, KG-RAG, OS-Symphony, Mobile-Agent-V, or the official Watch&Learn system; instead it uses an approximate raw-trajectory ICL control. This weakens the claim that the proposed structured annotation, rather than simply better retrieval/context engineering, is the key advance over prior work.

Some baselines are not fully comparable. For Qwen3-VL-8B, the no-annotation OSWorld baseline is taken from a prior report, with per-domain results unavailable, while other settings appear newly run under different retrieval, prompting, and environmental conditions. Given stochastic agents and network/task instability, this makes the reported +5.83 pp gain less clean than claimed.

The benefits of grounding are small and inconsistent. Planning accounts for most of the gain, while grounding-only is nearly neutral (+0.41 pp in Table 3) and full planning+grounding sometimes hurts domains or configurations relative to planning-only. This undercuts the paper’s strong dual-channel framing.

The evaluation lacks statistical confidence for the main full-benchmark results. Only a 120-task subset is averaged over three seeds; the headline OSWorld and WAA numbers appear to be single runs. Given noisy GUI-agent execution, API stochasticity, and reported network/model-output issues, confidence intervals or repeated full runs would be important.

The retrieval process may introduce benchmark-specific leakage or task overfitting concerns. The system searches the web at test time using the task and application, and OSWorld tasks are public. The paper does not sufficiently analyze whether retrieved videos overlap closely with benchmark tasks or whether the method is exploiting publicly available task-specific instructions rather than generalizable visual procedural learning.

Human evaluation mostly validates retrieval/topic filtering and the Meaningful filter, not the correctness or usefulness of the final planning and grounding knowledge. There is little direct assessment of hallucinated actions, wrong UI element descriptions, or whether the decomposed knowledge faithfully matches the video.

The cost and latency accounting is helpful but incomplete for practical use. The paper counts API cost but not the operational cost of downloading videos, Whisper/OmniParser compute, rate limits, failed downloads, legal/licensing constraints around YouTube content, or privacy/security implications of using live web videos during task execution.

The writing sometimes overclaims. Phrases such as “resolves domain bias,” “autonomous learning,” and “validating GUIDE as a scalable plug-and-play solution” are stronger than the evidence supports, especially given 82.8% retrieval coverage, notable failure cases, inconsistent domain results, and dependence on closed models.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and practically important problem: domain bias in GUI agents, especially the gap between general VLM capabilities and application-specific workflows/layouts. The framing into planning-level and grounding-level bias is clear and useful for the computer-use/GUI-agent community.

GUIDE is a well-motivated plug-and-play system rather than a narrow fine-tuning recipe. Its subtitle-driven Video-RAG pipeline, automated pairwise video annotation, and natural-language planning/grounding injection form a coherent contribution with clear applicability to existing single-model and multi-agent GUI agents.

The empirical evidence is fairly strong. The paper reports full OSWorld results over 361 tasks, improvements across Seed-1.8, Qwen3-VL-8B, and AgentS3 (+4.47 to +7.48 pp), and cross-benchmark transfer to WindowsAgentArena with large gains for both a strong multi-agent system and Qwen3-VL-32B.

The ablations and controls are above average: planning-only vs grounding-only, same-backbone Watch&Learn-style raw-trajectory ICL, subtitle-only and no-OmniParser variants, number of retrieved videos, retrieval matching controls, and human audits of retrieval/annotation quality. These make the main causal story more credible.

The paper is generally clear and reproducibility-conscious. It provides prompt structures, benchmark details, retrieval/annotation pipeline configuration, cost accounting, human evaluation statistics, and qualitative failure cases, including honest discussion of retrieval mismatch and grounding mismatch.
weaknesses: The method depends heavily on proprietary frontier models and live web resources: GPT-4.1/GPT-4.1-mini for retrieval, GPT-5.1 for annotation/decomposition, GPT-5.2 in one backbone, YouTube/yt-dlp availability, ASR, and OmniParser. This limits reproducibility, makes exact re-running fragile over time, and raises concerns about whether the approach remains effective under cheaper or fully open components at full scale.

The comparison to prior video-based GUI learning is helpful but not fully satisfying. The Watch&Learn-style baseline uses raw text trajectory ICL from the same retrieved videos, but it is not a full reproduction of Watch&Learn’s trained inverse-dynamics/retrieval setup. Thus the paper supports the value of structured decomposition over raw trajectory prompts, but less conclusively establishes superiority over the strongest existing video-learning pipelines.

The grounding contribution appears weaker than the framing suggests. Planning accounts for most of the gain, grounding-only gives only +0.41 pp on Qwen3-VL-8B, and adding grounding sometimes hurts domain scores. The paper acknowledges this, but the dual-channel claim would be stronger with more analysis of when grounding helps, when it misleads, and whether the UI-element descriptions are consistently used by agents.

Retrieval coverage and mismatch remain important limitations. Only 82.8% of OSWorld tasks retrieve at least one relevant tutorial, and the failure cases show that semantically adjacent but procedurally wrong videos can actively derail agents. The current safeguards of treating knowledge as reference material do not fully prevent harmful over-reliance.

Some evaluations use small subsets or unstable settings. The annotation component ablation uses 120 tasks, the K and annotator-model ablations use 50 tasks, and several per-domain numbers are non-monotonic. These are useful diagnostics, but the paper’s strongest claims should be interpreted through the full-benchmark results rather than the smaller exploratory ablations.

There are minor clarity and polish issues in the manuscript presentation, including dense tables, occasional formatting/extraction artifacts, and terminology that sometimes overstates the generality of the system given its dependence on live retrieval quality and proprietary annotation models. These do not undermine the core contribution but should be tightened.
